references.title: Prosody in Music and Songwriting
references.note: Teacher's article, one opinion with illustrative examples: prosody means every element supporting the central message; stable against unstable meaning; perfect, family and assonance rhyme. Not evidence.

references.title: The Best (and Worst) Romantic Song Lyrics
references.note: Teacher's reading of two songs: sense-bound language, line counts as feeling, an AABA form, and a pronoun switch he dislikes. Preferences are opinion.

references.title: Direct Address in Songwriting: Writing Lyrics That Feel Like Conversations
references.note: Course excerpt: lyrics between an I and a you, with gains, limits and four kinds of you. Craft vocabulary with song examples; no test of effect.

references.authors: Philip A. Fine and Jane Ginsborg
references.title: Making myself understood: perceived factors affecting the intelligibility of sung text
references.note: Survey of 143 musicians: 43 factors in four groups. Perceptions, not listener tests; gives no rule on open vowels, consonant clusters or breath.

references.title: Prominence matching in English songs: a historical perspective
references.note: Linguistics article on stress-to-beat matching in English text-setting, with a survey of about 90 songs from the 13th century to Shakespeare. Reports Dell and Halle, Halle and Lerdahl and Hayes and Kaun second-hand; descriptive, not a listener experiment, and no syllables-per-beat figure.

references.title: The metrics of folk song: text-setting in Spanish and English
references.note: Argument from two folk songs, one Spanish and one English, that English speech, verse and musical rhythm agree. Two songs and the stress-timed against syllable-timed typology; no corpus or experiment.

references.authors: Emilia Parada-Cabaleiro, Maximilian Mayerl, Stefan Brandl, Marcin Skowron, Markus Schedl, Elisabeth Lex and Eva Zangerle
references.title: Song lyrics have become simpler and more repetitive over the last five decades
references.note: 353,320 English lyrics from a user-edited site, 1970 to 2020: repeated-line ratio and chorus share rose in five genres. A trend in what exists, not a measure of quality; the abstract's wording says complexity decreased while the results show repetition increased.

references.authors: Lassi A. Liikkanen and Kelly Jakubowski
references.title: Involuntary musical imagery as a component of ordinary music cognition: a review of empirical evidence
references.note: Review of earworm studies. The chorus and lyrics figures (90% and 83%) are second-hand through the review; it calls hit song science results meager. About listening, not about writing.

references.authors: Joseph C. Nunes, Andrea Ordanini and Francesca Valsesia
references.title: The power of repetition: repetitive lyrics in a song increase processing fluency and drive market success
references.note: Abstract only: lab and chart studies of lexical repetition and fluency, with Billboard Hot 100 data 1958 to 2012. No sample sizes or effect sizes captured; chart data are observational.

references.title: Teleology in Verse-Prechorus-Chorus Form
references.note: Music-theory history of the prechorus in songs from 1965 to 2020: it builds toward an arrival at the chorus. About harmony, texture and form, not lyric lines per section.

references.title: Metre (hymn)
references.note: Weak evidence: an encyclopedia article, the only full set of hymn meter definitions read (Common, Long, Short, doubled, numbered). No allowed kind fits an encyclopedia, so the nearest is practitioner.

references.title: Tune: AZMON
references.note: One hymnal-database record: meter 8.6.8.6 with a link to more tunes of that meter, and the same tune recorded as 8686, CM and CMD. Not a definition of meter.

references.authors: Academy of American Poets (Hirsch, A Poet's Glossary)
references.title: Hymn (Glossary of Poetic Terms)
references.note: Glossary entry: the hymnal stanza, or common measure, is traditionally the same as the ballad stanza with stricter rhythms and rhymes. No syllable counts and no rule on matching texts to tunes.

references.title: Ballad stanza
references.note: Weak evidence: a short encyclopedia article giving the ballad stanza as four lines, iambic tetrameter then trimeter, rhymed ABCB. The nearest kind is practitioner.

references.title: Using automated rhyme detection to characterize rhyming style in rap music
references.note: Abstract only and about rap: imperfect and internal rhymes modelled statistically. No figures and nothing on pop or hymn lyrics.

references.title: Fair Use (FAQ)
references.note: Official general information, United States only and not legal advice: no legal rule permits a set number of words or notes, fair use depends on all the circumstances, and permission is recommended in cases of doubt.
